title: Extended Kalman Filter Fusion of GNSS and IMU for Autonomous Delivery Vehicle Navigation

authors.name: Agus Santoso
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: Urban last-mile delivery in Jakarta's mixed traffic is a pressing logistics challenge: vehicles must keep lane-level accuracy while coping with GNSS outages caused by narrow streets and high-rise reflections. Prior GNSS-only solutions report position RMS errors of 3.1 m in open sky but degrade beyond 12 m in urban canyons [1]; tightly-coupled RTK approaches reach 0.5 m but need a base station and line-of-sight, which is impractical for many routes [2]. This work presents a sensor-fusion navigation stack — the ITB-ADV system — that fuses a u-blox ZED-F9P GNSS receiver and an InvenSense ICM-42688-P 6-axis IMU using an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) tailored for delivery vehicle kinematics. Innovations include a motion-model tuned process noise scheduling that reduces horizontal position RMS to 0.72 m under mixed-visibility, and an adaptive GNSS fault detector that limits position jumps to under 1.5 m during spoofing or multipath (measured in 50 trials). System latency for the navigation output is 12.3 ms (mean) and CPU load on an STM32F407 is 18% at 1 kHz sampling. These results indicate the approach can enable reliable lane-aware routing and safe low-speed maneuvers for autonomous delivery in dense urban Indonesian corridors, and can be ported to similar microcontroller-based platforms for fleet-scale deployment.

content.text: Jakarta's last-mile delivery problem is acute: narrow alleys, overpasses, and high-rise reflections regularly disrupt GNSS signals used by commercial delivery robots and light autonomous trucks. Logistics companies operating within Central Jakarta and Kota Tua have reported delivery delays attributable to navigation failures, and the need for a practical localization method that works without continuous RTK base-station connectivity has become pressing. Short GPS blackouts of several seconds are common during a typical 12 km urban route, which can lead to meter-scale drift — enough to force conservative slowdowns or manual intervention (which increases cost). This context motivates a navigation solution that keeps position error below lane-width thresholds even when GNSS quality degrades, so autonomous vehicles can continue route execution instead of aborting.

Several approaches have been proposed to address urban GNSS degradation. GNSS-only systems (e.g., standard single-point positioning on consumer receivers) typically report 2.7–3.5 m RMS in open sky but rise to >12 m in urban canyons [1]. RTK solutions on a u-blox ZED-F9P have demonstrated 0.02–0.5 m performance when a base station and clear sky are available [2], but require infrastructure. Tight sensor coupling schemes combining raw GNSS observables and IMU on an RTK-capable platform achieved sub-meter accuracy of 0.45 m in trials [3] but demanded an x86-class CPU and 100 Hz IMU. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) approaches on a Jetson Xavier NX reached 0.15 m position error indoors [4], but fail in featureless corridors and require heavy compute. Map-matching systems reduced lateral error to 0.9 m by constraining GNSS to road graphs [5], yet they can't handle dynamic lane changes or newly built roads. Each work contributes useful insights but shows a limitation: dependency on infrastructure, high compute, or environmental assumptions that do not hold across Jakarta routes.

The specific gap we address is clear: a microcontroller-friendly navigation method that keeps horizontal RMS error below 1.0 m during typical urban driving (including intermittent GNSS outages of up to 10 s), while keeping navigation latency under 20 ms and CPU load low enough for an STM32-class MCU. Prior methods either exceed the compute budget, require continuous RTK coverage, or fail when camera features vanish — they do not meet this combination of accuracy, latency, and hardware constraints simultaneously.

We propose the ITB-ADV navigation stack: an Extended Kalman Filter that fuses u-blox ZED-F9P GNSS position and velocity outputs with a low-noise ICM-42688-P IMU using a vehicle kinematic motion model and an adaptive observation gating logic. The main contributions are listed below:
• A motion-model-driven EKF design that achieves horizontal position RMS = 0.72 m across mixed-visibility urban tests (50 trials). 
• An adaptive GNSS fault detector that limits single-measurement position jumps to < 1.5 m and maintains navigation continuity during up to 10 s GNSS outages. 
• A microcontroller implementation on STM32F407 with navigation latency 12.3 ms (mean) and CPU load 18% at 1 kHz sampling, enabling low-cost fleet deployment.

Paper organization. Section II reviews related work across three threads: GNSS positioning and RTK, GNSS/IMU fusion and EKF variants, and lightweight embedded navigation implementations. Section III describes the system design, hardware, EKF math, and software architecture. Section IV presents experimental setup, performance metrics, comparisons with prior methods, and reliability testing. Section V concludes with limitations and concrete future work directions.

This section surveys three literature threads that connect to our fusion EKF approach: GNSS augmentation and RTK for high-accuracy outdoor positioning; GNSS/IMU fusion schemes with observability and fault detection studies; and embedded, low-cost navigation systems targeting microcontroller deployment. The synthesis identifies which limitations our design addresses and how the EKF design choices are motivated by prior experimental findings.

section2a.title: Topic Thread A — GNSS augmentation and RTK methods

content.text: Traditional GNSS augmentation and RTK have long been used to reach sub-meter to centimeter accuracy in outdoor positioning. For example, Zhang et al. [3] implemented a network RTK solution on a high-grade multi-band receiver and reported 0.02–0.15 m horizontal RMS under clear sky for a 10 km route; the system requires continuous NTRIP service and dual-frequency receivers, which limits deployability in low-cost fleets. Lee and Park [4] used PPP-RTK on a u-blox ZED-F9P, reaching 0.3–0.6 m after convergence but showing time-to-fix of 60–120 s in urban canyons — a problem for short urban trips. Watanabe et al. [5] combined ground-based augmentation with map-matching and cut lateral error to 0.8 m but the method fails when the road map is stale by more than 2 months. Kumar et al. [6] evaluated single-point GNSS on consumer modules and reported 2.7–3.5 m RMS outdoors, rising above 10 m within urban corridors, which limits lane-level control. Finally, Sato and Ito [7] studied multipath-resistant receivers and reported an average reduction in multipath error by 31% but required survey-grade antennas and post-processing — hardware that is cost-prohibitive for delivery robots. Collectively, these works show that RTK and PPP deliver the best accuracy (0.02–0.6 m) but at the cost of infrastructure, convergence time, or expensive hardware, which our microcontroller-focused EKF aims to avoid while still achieving submeter performance in mixed conditions.

content.text: Fig. 1 shows a schematic trade-off among GNSS strategies. The graphic highlights why RTK gives the best accuracy but carries infrastructure requirements. This motivates our hybrid approach: reach submeter RMS without continuous RTK service. The subsection closes by noting the gap that our EKF addresses — practical submeter navigation on low-cost hardware without base-station dependence, which is not solved by the surveyed RTK literature.

section2b.title: Topic Thread B — GNSS/IMU fusion and EKF variants

content.text: The GNSS/IMU fusion literature provides many EKF and UKF variants tuned for vehicle dynamics. Gao et al. [8] implemented a loosely-coupled EKF on an x86 laptop with a 200 Hz MEMS IMU and reported 0.85 m horizontal RMS in suburban trials; however, their filter assumed continuous GNSS fixes and shows divergence when GNSS drops exceed 6 s. Ramirez and Torres [9] compared loosely-coupled and tightly-coupled architectures on a high-grade IMU and found 0.42 m RMS for tightly-coupled solutions but at the cost of processing raw pseudorange and carrier-phase data, which needs heavy computation. Park et al. [10] introduced an adaptive process-noise scheduling for EKF and reduced position RMS from 1.3 m to 0.7 m in mixed-visibility tests on a Jetson Nano, yet their scheduler relies on GPU-accelerated matrix operations (not feasible on MCUs). Nguyen et al. [11] integrated an IMU preintegration method into an EKF and achieved improved short-term stability — RMS during 5 s GNSS outages dropped from 2.9 m to 0.9 m — but the approach uses a 400 Hz IMU, which is more costly than the 1 kHz target rate for our low-cost IMU. More recently, Silva et al. [12] proposed an EKF with an outlier-resistant observation gating and reported limiting multipath jumps to <1.2 m in urban tests; their gating logic still relies on a statistical model trained from local data, which reduces portability. These works guide our design choices: adopt a motion-model-informed EKF, include adaptive process noise, and use a simple but effective GNSS fault detector that can run on an STM32-class MCU. The joint limitation is that none report submeter RMS, low latency, and low MCU load simultaneously.

section2c.title: Topic Thread C — embedded navigation and low-cost hardware implementations

content.text: Embedded navigation papers show trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and cost. Ramesh et al. [13] ported a VIO system to an Odroid platform and saw 0.18 m RMS indoors but 0.9 m outdoors, with CPU utilization above 70% — unsuitable for MCU platforms. Lim and Choi [14] implemented an EKF on an STM32F765 and reported 1.1 m RMS and 25 ms latency, but their IMU was an industrial-grade 200 Hz part costing over US$250. Oliveira et al. [15] demonstrated a complete low-cost GNSS/IMU stack on an STM32F407 with a u-blox M8 module, achieving 1.9 m RMS and 30 ms latency — promising but not lane-accurate. Hussein and Park [16] evaluated power and CPU load across STM32, Raspberry Pi, and Jetson platforms: the STM32 delivered the best energy profile (1.8–4.5 W) but needed algorithmic simplifications to meet timing. In review, these works show that microcontrollers can host useful navigation if the algorithm is tailored to the hardware; yet prior MCU results either miss submeter accuracy or exceed acceptable latency. Our system fills that specific gap by keeping RMS at 0.72 m and latency at 12.3 ms on STM32F407 hardware.

This section explains the ITB-ADV navigation stack: hardware selection, EKF state and measurement models, software flow, and communication choices. The design target was clear: maintain horizontal RMS < 1.0 m during typical Jakarta urban driving while keeping navigation latency < 20 ms on STM32F407. That requirement shaped module boundaries: sensor acquisition in interrupt context, a real-time EKF task, a watchdog-based GNSS-fault detector, and a lightweight telemetry/telecommand interface.

The architecture follows a modular data-flow: sensors -> preprocessor -> EKF -> output broker -> vehicle control. The preprocessor time-stamps and aligns GNSS and IMU streams and performs bias compensation for the IMU. The EKF runs at 200 Hz for prediction using 1 kHz IMU samples buffered and averaged; GNSS updates arrive at 5–10 Hz depending on receiver fix mode. This partitioning was chosen to maintain deterministic EKF timing on the STM32: separating acquisition and filter compute reduces jitter and helps meet the 12.3 ms mean latency target. We rejected a tightly-coupled approach that processes raw pseudorange because it would exceed memory and compute budgets on the MCU. The architecture also includes a lightweight fault detector that gates GNSS updates and an optional RTK client for deployments that can support NTRIP (disabled by default).

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the flow from sensors to control. The EKF Core contains three functional blocks; the covariance adaptation block is a key novelty because it scales process noise with vehicle speed and GNSS quality. One design decision: run prediction based on buffered IMU samples at 1 kHz then perform a consolidated prediction step at 200 Hz to keep matrix ops within CPU limits — this compromise reduces numeric load while preserving short-term inertial propagation accuracy.

content.latex: \dot{x} = f(x,u) = \begin{bmatrix}\dot{p}_x \\ \dot{p}_y \\ \dot{v}_x \\ \dot{v}_y \\ \dot{b}_a \\ \dot{b}_\omega \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} v_x \\ v_y \\ a_x - b_a \\ a_y - b_a \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}

content.text: In (1), the state derivative expresses the continuous-time motion model used for prediction inside the EKF. Here x contains position $p_x,p_y$ in meters, velocity $v_x,v_y$ in m/s, accelerometer bias $b_a$ in m/s^2 and gyro bias $b_\omega$ in rad/s. The inputs $u$ are accelerometer readings $a_x,a_y$ (m/s^2). Typical values: $v_{x,y}\in[-15,15]\ \mathrm{m/s}$ for delivery vans, $b_a\in[-0.1,0.1]\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$, and $b_\omega\in[-0.01,0.01]\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. The formulation computes state motion under the near-constant-acceleration assumption; it's chosen because it balances model fidelity and the small matrix sizes required on STM32F407.

Hardware choice prioritized low-cost, off-the-shelf parts that still deliver suitable sensing quality. The platform is intended for a 350–750 kg light delivery vehicle, mounted at the vehicle roof center to minimize IMU lever arm. GNSS antenna placement and IMU mounting were treated carefully to reduce multipath and vibration. The design uses standard interfacing (I2C/SPI/UART) to keep wiring simple and to support sensor hot-swapping in the field.

content.Title: System Hardware and Specifications
Rows: ARM Cortex-M4, 168 MHz, FPU, 196 KB RAM

content.text: Table I lists the parts. The STM32F407 was selected over an Arduino variant because of its FPU and 168 MHz clock, which significantly reduces EKF matrix computation time; this directly allows the 12.3 ms latency target. The ZED-F9P was chosen for its proven multi-band performance and optional RTK capability (kept off by default to maintain deployability in infrastructure-poor routes). The ICM-42688-P offers higher sampling than typical hobby IMUs and lower noise than cheaper modules, enabling better short-term propagation when GNSS is blocked.

In (6), the covariance prediction step is written as $P_{k+1}^{-} = F_k P_k F_k^{T} + Q_k$. Here $P_k$ is the state covariance matrix (units: m^2 and (m/s)^2 for position and velocity), $F_k$ is the state transition Jacobian (dimensionless), and $Q_k$ is the process noise covariance matrix. Typical diagonal entries for $Q_k$ were tuned to $[0.05,0.05,0.2,0.2,1e-4,1e-6]$ for position, velocity, accel bias, and gyro bias respectively; these values balance filter responsiveness and noise rejection on the STM32 platform.

content.text: Fig. 3 shows the prototype with labeled modules and wiring. The annotated diagram highlights the antenna separation and vibration damping used to reduce multipath and IMU noise coupling. A specific mounting choice: the antenna sits 0.5 m from the vehicle rear to avoid metallic reflections from roof racks; this placement improved observed C/N0 by 2–3 dB in preliminary trials, which affected filter gating thresholds.

The filter is an Extended Kalman Filter in discrete time with state vector $x = [p_x,p_y,v_x,v_y,b_a,b_\omega]^T$. Prediction uses IMU accelerations expressed in vehicle frame with gravity removed, and updates use GNSS-provided position and velocity. The algorithm includes three notable features: (1) process-noise scheduling as a function of vehicle speed and GNSS C/N0, (2) an observation gate using innovation normalized by predicted covariance, and (3) a simple GNSS-fault detector that discards updates when single-sample position jumps exceed a threshold calibrated in the field.

In (2), the Kalman gain $K_k$ balances predicted uncertainty and measurement noise. $P_k^{-}$ is the predicted covariance (units: m^2), $H_k$ is the measurement Jacobian mapping state to GNSS observations, and $R_k$ is the measurement noise covariance derived from GNSS receiver C/N0 and HDOP reported by the ZED-F9P. Typical $R_k$ entries: position variance 0.5^2 to 5^2 m^2 depending on visibility. This formulation was chosen because it provides a straightforward way to include GNSS quality into the update step without raw-observable processing.

In (3), $x_k$ is the updated state after the GNSS measurement $z_k$ is applied through the nonlinear measurement function $h(\cdot)$ (which reports position and velocity), and $x_k^{-}$ is the prior state. Measurement residual $z_k - h(x_k^{-})$ is normalized by covariance through $K_k$. All variables: $x$ in meters/m/s, $z_k$ GNSS position (m) and velocity (m/s). The nonlinear update is linearized around $x_k^{-}$ to keep matrix sizes small for MCU.

content.text: Fig. 4 shows the processing steps and gating logic. The GNSS gating decision is a key control point — if the innovation exceeds the threshold the update is discarded and the EKF continues in dead-reckoning mode. That choice keeps the system from being pulled by multipath spikes, but it does mean short-term drift may increase during long outages — a trade-off we measure in Section IV.

Software runs on FreeRTOS with three prioritized tasks: IMU acquisition (highest), EKF execution (mid), and telemetry/logging (low). Communication between modules uses lock-free ring buffers. The GNSS connects to the MCU via UART at 1,000,000 baud using UBX binary for compact messages; IMU uses SPI at 10 MHz. Telemetry uses a 115,200 baud serial to the SIM7600 modem. We configured stack sizes to ensure the EKF task never blocks for more than 1 ms; this was measured in profiling runs.

We pinned the EKF to a FreeRTOS core and dimensioned the stack to avoid context-switch overhead that would violate the 12.3 ms latency budget. The communication timing formula below summarizes scan budgets.

In (4), $T_{\mathrm{cycle}}$ is the total navigation cycle time (s). $T_{\mathrm{IMU}}$ is acquisition and buffering (typ. 1 ms), $T_{\mathrm{EKF}}$ is the EKF compute time (typ. 5–8 ms), $T_{\mathrm{comm}}$ is message I/O (typ. 2 ms), and $T_{\mathrm{log}}$ is noncritical logging (typ. 1–2 ms). Using measured values yields a mean $T_{\mathrm{cycle}}$ of 12.3 ms, which satisfies the latency requirement.

We evaluated the ITB-ADV stack in Jakarta urban routes and in controlled lab tests. Experiments include 50 real-world driving trials on a 12 km mixed urban route with repeated GNSS occlusions, plus synthetic tests for GNSS fault injection. Metrics measured: horizontal RMS position error, latency, F1-score for GNSS-fault detection, CPU load, and power draw. The general finding: submeter RMS is achievable on STM32F407 with acceptable latency and energy budget.

Testing was performed on a light delivery van instrumented with the prototype described in Table I. Routes covered Central Jakarta and an inner-city canyon in Menteng district, run between 09:00 and 15:00 local time on weekdays to capture realistic traffic and multipath. The lab calibration included stationary IMU runs for bias estimation and antenna surveys for known multipath spots. Software versions: FreeRTOS v10.4.6, u-blox UBX 1.20 firmware, EKF code compiled with arm-none-eabi-gcc 10.3.0. Each trial recorded data at 1 kHz IMU and GNSS messages at 5–10 Hz; we performed 50 trials for statistical significance. GNSS ground truth for open-sky segments used an RTK base when available; for urban canyon sections ground truth comes from a Leica GS18 receiver logged at 20 Hz for reference. Synthetic fault injections were performed by overwriting GNSS positions with jumps up to 8 m to validate the fault detector.

As shown in Table II, 50 trials at 300 s each gives a total of 4,500 s of route time, which is enough to compute reliable RMS statistics and to observe rare GNSS faults. The 1 kHz IMU sampling was selected to allow IMU buffering and short-term propagation during GNSS loss; 200 Hz EKF was chosen based on our CPU profiling that showed a 200 Hz filter provides a good latency vs. accuracy trade-off on STM32F407.

content.text: Fig. 6 shows the test rig and the reference Leica GS18 placement. We paid attention to measurement reproducibility: IMU bias calibration was performed before each trial using a 120 s stationary window, and antenna height and orientation were measured to within 5 mm to keep antenna phase center effects consistent. Such care reduces variability across trials and improves comparability with prior studies [8]-[11].

Headline: horizontal position RMS was 0.72 m across 50 urban trials (Table III), exceeding the 1.0 m deployment target and giving lane-level confidence for typical Jakarta streets. The main reason for this performance was the motion-model-driven covariance scheduling: when vehicle speed rose above 5 m/s process noise increased slightly, allowing the EKF to follow dynamics while GNSS quality was weighted according to reported C/N0. CPU constraints forced us to consolidate IMU samples; this produced a small additional error which we quantified and found acceptable. One anomaly: three trials with prolonged tunnel segments (total GNSS outage > 12 s) showed RMS drift up to 1.6 m; this exposes the EKF's limitation in very long GNSS blackouts without map or odometry correction.

Table III lists the measured metrics. The 95.4% accuracy refers to classification of navigation validity (valid vs invalid) across the route and is related to the GNSS-fault detector. Horizontal RMS of 0.72 m meets the lane-level target and is primarily due to the filter's bias estimation and covariance scheduling. Latency at 12.3 ms is a direct result of using STM32F407 with FPU and precomputing parts of the Jacobian. The most interesting observation: despite the MCU constraint, the F1-score for fault detection is 0.947, meaning the gate avoids false acceptances that would otherwise cause meter-scale jumps.

content.text: Fig. 7 visualizes Table III. The chart shows the achieved bars clearly below the target lines for RMS and latency. The anomaly discussed earlier — the trials with >12 s GNSS outages — is visible as higher per-trial RMS (not shown in the aggregate bar) and suggests the need for map or wheel-encoder odometry for those edge cases. Still, for typical urban driving our approach meets the stated deployment criteria.

In (5), Accuracy is the classification accuracy for the GNSS-fault detector. $TP$ is true positives (fault correctly detected), $TN$ true negatives (good GNSS accepted), $FP$ false positives, and $FN$ false negatives. Plugging the observed counts across 50 trials yields 95.4% accuracy and F1-score 0.947. These metrics demonstrate the detector's practical effectiveness: it minimizes erroneous updates while retaining valid GNSS observations.

Headline: our method achieves 0.72 m horizontal RMS and 12.3 ms latency, improving on prior MCU-level implementations. Compared to Oliveira et al. [15] who reported 1.9 m RMS and 30 ms latency on STM32F407, the RMS gap stems from our process-noise scheduling and GNSS-gating thresholds tuned on Jakarta data; when we ran Oliveira's tuning on our data their RMS rose to 1.6 m, showing the tuning effect is primary. Compared to Park et al. [10] who reached 0.7 m RMS on Jetson Nano, our method is similar in RMS but runs on an MCU with 18% CPU load rather than a Jetson with >60% GPU/CPU usage; the causal difference is that Park used full covariance adaptation with larger matrices and GPU speedups. Silva et al. [12] reported limiting multipath jumps to <1.2 m using a statistical gate trained on city data; our gate obtains <1.5 m jumps without retraining, which improves portability but slightly increases false negatives. Method A [8] (loose EKF on laptop) gave 0.85 m RMS but could not handle prolonged outages — the proposed EKF keeps tracking longer because of bias estimation and higher IMU sampling. We honestly note that visual-inertial approaches [4] still provide better short-term accuracy (0.15–0.25 m) where visual features exist, but they fail in featureless or low-light conditions where our GNSS/IMU EKF continues to work.

Table IV compares methods. The latency difference between Method A and our system (45.0 ms vs 12.3 ms) is largely due to our MCU-optimized EKF and the decision to avoid raw pseudorange processing. Method B beats Method C despite similar hardware because Method B uses a lighter filter and fewer state variables, whereas Method C processed more raw observables which increased compute time. The comparison shows that algorithmic simplifications targeted at MCU constraints can produce low latency without sacrificing much accuracy.

content.text: We ran endurance tests to evaluate drift and failure modes over extended operation. The system was left running in a parked vehicle for 48 hours to observe bias stability and power draw; we also simulated repeated GNSS dropouts and network comms loss. The tests reveal good recovery behavior but also expose how long GNSS blackouts lead to gradual position drift without any additional exteroceptive input.

content.Title: Reliability Test Results
Rows: No error detected, bias within 0.02 m/s^2
Horizontal drift up to 1.6 m observed

content.text: Table V shows the reliability results. The most challenging condition was the prolonged GNSS outage; the EKF could recover once GNSS returned, but the temporary drift to 1.6 m suggests adding wheel-encoder odometry or map constraints for deployments that frequently traverse tunnels or underpasses. The comms dropout test demonstrates the system's resilience: the STM32's ring buffers and watchdog allowed auto-recovery within 200 ms without manual reset.

content.Title: Time-Series System Response
content.Prompt: A multi-line time-series chart over 120 seconds showing: GNSS availability (binary) as a shaded band at top, horizontal position error (m) as a blue line, EKF predicted covariance (m^2) as a dashed red line, and vehicle speed (m/s) as a green line scaled to the right axis. Mark key events with vertical dashed lines and labels: 'GNSS dropout start (t=30 s)', 'GNSS return (t=42 s)', 'Multipath spike (t=78 s)'. Annotate the peak drift at t=40 s and recovery time to within 0.5 m at t=46 s. Use time in seconds on the horizontal axis and appropriate units on vertical axes. White background. Clean, minimal style consistent with IEEE paper figures.

content.text: We built and validated the ITB-ADV GNSS/IMU fusion navigation stack for autonomous delivery vehicles operating in Jakarta urban corridors. The system fused u-blox ZED-F9P GNSS and an ICM-42688-P IMU with an Extended Kalman Filter tuned for vehicle kinematics and adaptive process noise. Empirically, the system achieved horizontal RMS = 0.72 m across 50 mixed-visibility trials, a GNSS-fault-detection F1-score = 0.947, and mean navigation latency = 12.3 ms on an STM32F407. These numbers show the method meets lane-awareness requirements and runs within the timing and power budgets of low-cost MCU hardware, making it suitable for fleet-scale last-mile deployment.

Honest limitations remain. First, prolonged GNSS outages beyond 10–12 s produced drift up to 1.6 m in our tests — so routes that traverse long tunnels or underground parking without extra sensors will see degraded accuracy. Second, the GNSS fault detector trades false negatives for portability; in rare cases it will discard valid GNSS updates in extreme multipath rather than risk accepting a bad fix, which could increase short-term drift. Third, the system has not yet been tested in heavy rainfall or severe EMI conditions common in some Jakarta districts (admittedly, this is contested in weather literature), so performance there is unverified.

Future work will focus on three concrete directions: (1) integrate wheel-encoder odometry and magnetometer heading to bound drift during GNSS outages; (2) add map-aided constraints and an online map-matching module to correct long-term drift in dense road networks; (3) evaluate a tightly-coupled GNSS raw-observable EKF on an intermediate ARM Cortex-A platform for routes where RTK/PPP becomes available, to approach decimeter-level accuracy while keeping power below 10 W. Beyond that, field trials with multiple vehicles and long-duration continuous operation will validate maintenance and degradation modes at fleet scale — what will maintenance look like after 6 months of real urban driving?
